items.title: The Great Storm of October 1987
items.summary: A rapidly deepening Atlantic depression brought destructive winds to northern France and southern England on the night of 15–16 October 1987. It crossed England from the south-west towards the Humber, with the worst winds in south-east England before dawn. Fallen trees, damaged buildings and disrupted power and transport affected a densely populated region. The storm prompted changes to British weather observations, forecasting and the delivery of severe weather warnings.

impacts.text: The Met Office reports 18 deaths in England. Its account does not separate direct from indirect deaths.
The Forestry Commission estimated that 15 million trees were blown down. At the peak of the power cuts, 3 million householders and businesses were without electricity.
Fallen trees blocked roads and railways and brought down telephone and electricity lines. Buildings and boats were damaged; a Channel ferry was driven ashore near Folkestone.
In France, the damaging winds swept north through Brittany and Normandy before reaching the northern coast. Ports and forests were damaged, and some wind recorders failed or reached their limits.

history.text: Forecast models increasingly placed the severe weather south of England. Evening broadcasts stressed heavy rain, although warnings reached emergency authorities. At 0135 UTC, 16 October, the Met Office warned the Ministry of Defence that civil authorities might need military assistance.

After the storm, more ocean buoys improved observations around the British Isles. The Met Office also established the National Severe Weather Warning Service to coordinate warnings for government, emergency responders, industry and the public.

why_interesting.text: This was an extratropical depression, despite its association with hurricane-force winds. It developed along a strong contrast between cold polar air and warm, moist air, then moved rapidly across England. The Forestry Commission places the strongest-wind sector over south-east England between 03.00 and 06.00 GMT on 16 October.

Browning’s later study connected damaging winds in this storm with the hooked tip of its cloud head beside a dry slot. This became a key case for understanding the sting jet: a small region of particularly strong winds within some extratropical cyclones. The surface gust pattern alone cannot establish its presence.

items.reanalysis: ERA5 follows a deep low from west of Iberia across the western Channel and England towards the North Sea: its centre is 953 hPa near 49.21°N, 4.60°W at 00 UTC 16 Oct. Its minimum is 951 hPa near 48.13°N, 6.06°W at 22 UTC 15 Oct, earlier than the contemporary midnight analyses. The strongest gust in the displayed region is 42 m/s east of East Anglia, near 52.50°N, 2.25°E, in the hour ending 07 UTC 16 Oct. At Pointe du Roc, ERA5 peaks at 35 m/s in the hour ending 01 UTC 16 Oct; its much lower gusts than the published observations likely reflect smoothing of coastal exposure and narrow wind maxima on the 0.25° grid.

era5_vs_observed.quantity: Central pressure: minimum and midnight analysis
era5_vs_observed.era5: Minimum 951 hPa at 22 UTC 15 Oct, near 48.13°N, 6.06°W; 953 hPa at 00 UTC 16 Oct, near 49.21°N, 4.60°W.
era5_vs_observed.observed: Burt and Mansfield analyse about 953 hPa at 0000 GMT 16 October between Cornwall and Brittany. The Forestry Commission gives 952 hPa at 00.00 GMT north-west of Brittany. These are analyses, rather than readings at one station.

era5_vs_observed.quantity: Strongest gust: regional maximum and Pointe du Roc
era5_vs_observed.era5: Regional maximum 42.1 m/s near 52.50°N, 2.25°E, in the hour ending 07 UTC 16 Oct. At Pointe du Roc (48.85°N, 1.62°W), the maximum is 34.9 m/s in the hour ending 01 UTC 16 Oct.
era5_vs_observed.observed: Burt and Mansfield report a measured 117 knots (about 60 m/s) at Pointe du Roc at 0030 GMT 16 October. Météo-France says its cliff-top recorder reached its 216 km/h limit, so this does not establish an uncensored peak. The regional ERA5 maximum is at a different place and time.

era5_vs_observed.era5: 40.1 m/s at the sampled Shoreham location (50.83°N, 0.27°W), in the hour ending 04 UTC 16 Oct.
era5_vs_observed.observed: Burt and Mansfield list a measured 98 knots at 0310 and 0330 GMT 16 October, and a probable 100 knots during 04–05 GMT when power was lost. The Met Office instead lists 100 knots at 3.10 am, without stating the time zone. The measured and estimated values are distinct.

era5_vs_observed.era5: 37.5 m/s at the sampled Gatwick location (51.15°N, 0.18°W), in the hour ending 04 UTC 16 Oct.
era5_vs_observed.observed: Measured 86 knots (about 44 m/s) at Gatwick at 0430 GMT 16 October, according to Burt and Mansfield. The airport closed.

era5_vs_observed.era5: Lowest pressure 952.9 hPa at the sampled Ouessant location (48.46°N, 5.06°W), at 23 UTC 15 Oct.
era5_vs_observed.observed: Météo-France’s Brittany report records a barometer minimum of 948 hPa at Ouessant during the 15–16 October storm. It gives no observation time or time zone; this cannot be treated as a simultaneous comparison.
